title: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
summary: How an alert storm collapses to one page, how the four golden signals read as distributions, how a dependency graph and change correlation narrow six services to one, and how postmortems stop a repeat.
outcomes: Reduce an alert storm with deduplication, grouping and inhibition, and explain what suppression can hide
Read latency as a distribution during an incident and infer which dependency a bimodal tail points at
Walk a dependency graph to the anomalous frontier and rule candidates out by magnitude and saturation
Use change correlation and bisection over deploys and config pushes, and compute the number of tests needed
Separate trigger, proximate cause and contributing factors, and write action items that cut a named condition

lessons.title: One fault, 397 alerts: collapsing the storm

blocks.md:
At 20:16 your phone lights up. Over the next ninety seconds, 397 alerts fire across five services: latency alerts, error-ratio alerts, a saturation alert, an SLO burn alert (an SLO is a reliability target such as 99.9 percent of checkouts under 300 ms, and a burn alert fires when that budget is being spent too fast). Nothing in that list says which service is broken. One fault produced all of them.

This is called an *alert storm*: a single failure triggers a mass of correlated alerts that can all be traced back to a few causes, but whose sheer number makes manual handling hopeless (see [Knowledge-aware Alert Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06485), which studies exactly this problem on a production cloud platform). The first skill of root cause analysis is not deduction. It is refusing to read 397 alerts.

We will work one incident for the whole course, with every number computed from a stated model so you can check it.

The system is a checkout path with five services and one database:

- **edge** takes 2000 requests per second; 45 percent of them enter checkout.
- **checkout** takes 900 rps and calls **cart** and **pricing** in parallel, then spends 5 ms of its own.
- **cart** answers in about 22 ms and talks to a session store.
- **pricing** spends 18 ms of its own work; 60 percent of its requests hit a local price cache, and the other 40 percent (360 rps) call **catalog**.
- **catalog** answers each request with one 12 ms database query, taken from a connection pool of 64. Pricing gives up on a catalog call after 1000 ms.

blocks.title: The checkout path, and where the 397 alerts fired

scenes.caption: The dependency graph. Checkout fans out to cart and pricing in parallel, so its latency is the maximum of the two, not the sum.
Replica counts. Each service runs many pods, and most alert rules fire once per pod, which is where large alert counts come from.
Alerts firing at 20:17. Two rules per service on checkout, pricing and catalog, one each on edge and cart: 396 instance alerts, plus one service-level SLO burn alert.
After grouping by alert name and service, 9 notifications remain. Only the SLO burn on the user-facing checkout path pages a human; the other 8 land in the incident channel as context.

blocks.md:
The reduction happens in four mechanical steps, all of which exist in [Prometheus Alertmanager](https://prometheus.io/docs/alerting/latest/alertmanager/):

1. **Deduplication.** Two Prometheus replicas each evaluate the same rules and both send, so 794 notifications arrive for 397 distinct alerts. Alerts with identical labels are one alert.
2. **Grouping.** Alerts of similar nature become a single notification. Grouping by alert name and service turns 397 into 9. The docs give the same example: hundreds of instances alert when they lose the database, and you want one page that still lists who was affected.
3. **Inhibition.** Firing alert A mutes alert B. The documented pattern is coarse and safe: if an entire cluster is unreachable, mute every alert about that cluster.
4. **Silences.** A human mutes matching alerts for a stated time, usually during a known maintenance.

scenes.caption: Two Prometheus replicas evaluate the same rules during the fault, so 794 notifications are sent for the same event.
Deduplication by label set removes the replica copies: 397 distinct alerts remain. No information is lost.
Grouping by alert name and service: 9 notifications. The per-pod detail is still inside each group, just not on your phone.
Routing: only the checkout SLO burn alert pages. One human, one page, with 8 groups of context attached.

blocks.md: Dedup and grouping are lossless: they change how many notifications you receive, not what was observed. Inhibition and silences are lossy: they delete evidence from your view. Use the first two freely and the last two sparingly.

It is tempting to write inhibition rules along the dependency graph (if catalog is unhealthy, mute pricing and checkout). Google's own monitoring chapter reports only limited success with complex dependency hierarchies and keeps such rules to very stable parts of the system, such as muting latency alerts for a datacenter that has been drained on purpose. A stale dependency rule can mute the one alert that named the cause.

The storm itself carries information. In Cloudflare's [2 July 2019 outage](https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-july-2-2019/), a WAF rule deployed at 13:42 exhausted CPU on every machine serving HTTP traffic. The first page landed three minutes later from a synthetic WAF test, followed by failing end-to-end tests of other services, a global traffic drop alert, widespread 502 errors, and CPU exhaustion reports from points of presence worldwide. Their write-up is explicit that alerts of limited, local scope are handled many times a day, but that *this pattern* of pages meant something gravely serious, so the team declared a P0 immediately.

Shape matters more than count: alerts from one service means one service, alerts from every service at once means something shared.

blocks.prompt: During the same fault, cart also fired an alert (its p99 crossed a 40 ms threshold) even though nothing downstream of cart changed. Before reading on: does that make cart a suspect, a victim, or neither?
blocks.reveal: Neither, yet. Cart is not downstream of the broken service and nothing routes through it from pricing, so it cannot be a victim of this fault; and its p99 moved from 33 ms to 41 ms, which cannot explain a 1023 ms symptom. It turns out cart shipped a deploy at 20:09, five minutes before the real change. Lesson 4 shows how that coincidence cost six minutes of triage. Two changes in one window is the normal case, not a trick.

blocks.question: Your Alertmanager groups by alert name only, not by service. During this incident the group named ServiceLatencyHigh contains alerts from checkout, pricing, catalog and cart. What have you lost?
options: Nothing: grouping is lossless, and the labels are still in the notification
The error-ratio alerts, because grouping keeps only one alert type per group
The ability to see at a glance which services are affected and which are not, because one group now hides the per-service pattern that points at the cause
The SLO burn alert, which is always inhibited by instance-level alerts
blocks.explain: Grouping is lossless in principle (the labels travel with the group), but the grouping key decides what the notification shows you first. Grouping by name alone merges unrelated services into one blob and destroys exactly the signal you want: which parts of the graph are anomalous. Group by something that preserves topology, such as alert name plus service or cluster.

blocks.question: A team is paged 40 times a night and silences most alerts by reflex. Which failure mode does the SRE monitoring chapter warn about specifically?
options: Real pages get skimmed or ignored because they are masked by noise, so outages last longer
Alertmanager drops alerts once a silence is active, so the data is gone from the time series too
Dedup stops working when the alert volume is high
Grouping becomes lossy above roughly 100 alerts per group
blocks.explain: The chapter is blunt about this: when pages come too often, people second-guess, skim or ignore them, and real pages get masked by the noise, which prolongs outages. Silences mute notifications only; the underlying time series is untouched. The other two claims are inventions.

lessons.title: The four golden signals, read as distributions

blocks.md:
With one page in hand you need numbers. The monitoring chapter of the SRE book names four signals to carry for any user-facing system, the *four golden signals*:

- **Latency**, the time to serve a request, with successful and failed requests kept apart (a fast error and a slow error mean different things, and folding 500s into your latency makes it meaningless).
- **Traffic**, demand on the system, in a system-specific unit such as requests per second.
- **Errors**, the rate of failing requests: explicitly (a 500), implicitly (a 200 with wrong content), or by policy (slower than your stated limit counts as failed).
- **Saturation**, how full the service is in whatever resource constrains it, remembering that most systems degrade well before 100 percent utilization.

Here are those signals for our incident at 20:17, three minutes after the fault began, computed from the model in lesson 1.

- **catalog**: p50 1000 ms, p99 1000 ms, errors 7.41 percent, pool utilization 1.08.
- **pricing**: p50 18 ms, p99 1018 ms, mean 400 ms, errors 2.96 percent.
- **checkout**: p50 29 ms, p99 1023 ms, mean 408 ms, errors 2.96 percent.
- **edge**: p50 10 ms, p90 1025 ms, mean 187 ms, errors 1.33 percent.
- **cart**: p50 24 ms, p99 41 ms, errors 0.02 percent.

Read the medians. Pricing's median is 18 ms, exactly its healthy value. Catalog's median is 1000 ms, 83 times its healthy value. Those two facts, by themselves, almost solve the incident.

blocks.title: One checkout request, before and during the fault

scenes.caption: Healthy cache miss, 40 percent of pricing requests: catalog answers in 12 ms, pricing in 30 ms, checkout at p99 in 38 ms.
Same path at 20:17. The catalog request now waits 988 ms in the pool queue before its 12 ms query, so pricing returns 1018 ms and checkout 1023 ms. Earlier timings stay on screen for comparison.
For 7.41 percent of catalog calls the wait would exceed the 1000 ms timeout, so pricing abandons the call and fails the quote. These are slow errors: they cost a full second before failing.

blocks.md: Now the distributions. Pricing serves 900 rps. During the fault 540 of them hit the cache and finish in 18 ms, and 333 of them wait out the catalog queue and finish in 1018 ms; the remaining 27 fail at the timeout. Bucket the successful ones into latency histogram buckets (the SRE book recommends roughly exponential boundaries) and the shape is unmistakable.

blocks.title: Pricing latency histogram: successful requests per second

scenes.caption: Healthy: 540 rps of cache hits at 18 ms, 360 rps of misses at 30 ms. One narrow mode, p99 of 30 ms.
At 20:17 the miss mass has moved to the far right: 333 rps at 1018 ms. The hit mass has not moved at all, which is why the median is still 18 ms.
The mean is 400 ms, which lands in the 300-1000 ms bucket. That bucket holds zero requests. No request was ever served in 400 ms.

blocks.caption: A bimodal distribution puts the mean in a gap between the modes. The prerequisite course made this point for the tail; during an incident it goes further: the mean hides both which requests are fine and how slow the bad ones are.

blocks.md: The shape names the suspect. A mass of requests piled at exactly the client timeout means a dependency that is not answering. The *size* of that mass is the fraction of traffic that touches it: pricing's slow mass is 40 percent of its requests, which is exactly its cache miss rate, so the suspect is whatever a cache miss does. A distribution that shifts as a whole, like catalog's, means the service itself is queueing.

That whole-distribution shift is the saturation signal. Catalog's resource is its connection pool, and the number of requests in flight follows Little's law, $L = \lambda W$: at 360 rps with a mean of 1 second in the service, 360 requests are in flight against a pool of 4. Utilization is

pool utilization = (360 requests per second) x (12 ms per query) / (4 connections) = 1.08

Above 1.0 the queue has no steady state, so it grows until requests hit the timeout and are shed. Below 1.0 the queue is stable, but the mean wait climbs steeply as utilization approaches 1, which is why services degrade well before full utilization. That is why a pool size is a cliff rather than a slope.

blocks.title: Queue wait at catalog versus pool size

curves.label: mean wait, capped at the 1000 ms timeout

scenes.caption: At 360 rps the cliff sits at 4.32 connections. A pool of 64, or 16, or 8 all look identical and healthy; a pool of 4 is on the wrong side of it. Simplified: this uses a single-queue waiting-time formula, so treat the curve as the shape, not a prediction.
Drag the load down to 280 rps and the same pool of 4 is fine. The config value was never wrong by itself; it was wrong for this load.

At 480 rps the cliff moves to 5.76 connections, so a pool of 5 falls off it while a pool of 6 sits just on the edge at about 50 ms. This is why a saturation signal has to be a ratio of load to capacity, not a fixed threshold on either one.

blocks.question: Edge reports mean latency 188 ms, median 10 ms, p90 1025 ms. Another engineer says the edge is slow and wants to scale it. What do these three numbers actually say?
options: The edge is saturated, since the mean is 19 times the median
A minority of edge requests (about 17 percent) are extremely slow while the majority are untouched, so the fault is on a path that only some requests take
The edge has a latency distribution typical of a healthy service under load
The p90 is unreliable at this traffic level and should be ignored
blocks.explain: The median being unchanged rules out anything that affects all edge requests, and a p90 at 1025 ms with a p50 at 10 ms puts a large mass far to the right. In the model 45 percent of edge traffic enters checkout and 37 percent of those are slow, so 16.7 percent of edge requests sit at the top mode. Scaling the edge would add capacity to the part that is working.

blocks.question: Pricing's errors are requests abandoned at the 1000 ms timeout. Why does the SRE book insist you track the latency of failed requests separately rather than filtering them out?
options: Because failed requests always take longer than successful ones
Because percentiles cannot be computed from a mixed population
Because errors can be served very fast (a 500 from a failed connection) which drags your latency figure down, while a slow error is worse for the user than a fast one
Because error latency is the only way to compute an error budget
blocks.explain: The chapter gives both directions: an HTTP 500 caused by a dead backend may return in a millisecond and flatter your latency numbers, and a slow error is worse than a fast error, so you want error latency in its own right. Here every error costs a full second before failing, which is both a user-visible cost and a strong clue (the value equals the configured timeout).

blocks.question: Which single measurement best distinguishes the hypothesis that catalog is itself saturated from the hypothesis that catalog's database got slow?
options: Catalog's p99 latency, which is 1000 ms either way
Catalog's error rate of 7.41 percent
The number of catalog pods firing alerts
Catalog's pool wait time against its database query time: 988 ms waiting for a connection versus 12 ms executing the query
blocks.explain: p99, error rate and alert count are identical under both hypotheses, so none of them discriminates. Splitting the latency into time spent waiting for a resource and time spent doing work does: the query still takes 12 ms, so the database is fine and the backlog is in front of the pool. Instrument the wait and the work separately, or you cannot tell these apart during an incident.

lessons.title: Walking the dependency graph to the anomalous frontier

blocks.md:
Five services are anomalous and four of them are innocent. The standard move is to walk the dependency graph from the symptom downward and keep only the deepest anomalous nodes.

Call $A$ the set of anomalous services and $\mathrm{deps}(v)$ the services $v$ calls. The candidate set is the *anomalous frontier*: nodes that are anomalous but whose own dependencies are all healthy. If a service is slow and everything it calls is fine, the problem is in that service.

blocks.caption: The anomalous frontier. This is the same intuition that graph-based research tools encode: localize to the node whose anomaly is not explained by a downstream anomaly.

scenes.caption: Baseline at 20:13, p99 per service. Everything is inside its objective.
At 20:17, five of seven nodes are anomalous. Walking down from the symptom alone does not pick a winner: four services are slow because of someone else.
Apply the frontier rule. Edge, checkout and pricing each have an anomalous dependency, so each anomaly is already explained. They drop out.
Two candidates left. The magnitude test kills cart: checkout waits on the slower of cart and pricing, so even a cart answering in 0 ms leaves checkout at 1023 ms. Cart cannot produce the symptom.

Inside catalog: the database still answers in 12 ms at the normal 360 queries per second, and the backlog sits in front of the connection pool. The cause is catalog's own configuration, not its database.

blocks.md:
In practice you do not do this by eye. You lay the per-service signals next to each other and apply the three tests in order: is the node anomalous, are its dependencies anomalous, and can its size explain the symptom.

Saturation in that table is in-flight work from Little's law divided by each service's own concurrency limit. Only catalog's limit, the pool of 4, comes from the model in lesson 1; the other four rows use each service's configured limit.

blocks.title: Signal table at 20:17: p99, errors, saturation, change

scenes.caption: The four columns are p99 latency in ms, error rate in percent, saturation of the constraining resource, and whether a change landed in the window. Saturation is in-flight work over the limit, from Little's law.
Anomalous cells in red. Four services breach latency and error objectives; cart breaches only its tight 40 ms latency rule.
Frontier rule: keep only rows whose dependencies are healthy. Edge, checkout and pricing are out; cart and catalog remain, and both had a change in the window.
Only one candidate has a saturated resource, and only one has a p99 large enough to produce a 1023 ms symptom. Catalog's pool utilization of 1.08 is the single cell that explains everything above it.

blocks.md: Correlation is not causation, and the SRE troubleshooting chapter names the two ways this bites. First, correlated events often share a cause: packet loss in a cluster and failed disks in the same cluster correlate because a power event hit both, not because either caused the other. Second, as you monitor more metrics it becomes inevitable that some will correlate well with your symptom purely by coincidence.

The graph walk is only as good as the graph. Three ways it misleads you:

- **Missing edges.** Shared hosts, shared caches, a shared network path and a shared config service couple services that your service map shows as unrelated. The frontier rule then declares two unrelated nodes to be causes.
- **Wrong direction.** Retries and backpressure push effects upstream. A client that retries aggressively can saturate the dependency it is complaining about, so the frontier node is a victim of its own callers.
- **Stale edges.** Graphs built by hand rot. Graphs built from traces or from recent RPC samples do not, which is why Google servers expose endpoints listing the RPCs a task recently sent and received, so you can see the real topology without trusting a diagram.

Research in this area automates exactly these steps, and reading it tells you what the hard part is.

- [Sieve](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.06686) reduces thousands of monitored metrics by at least an order of magnitude and then infers dependencies between components by testing for Granger causality, a predictive-causality test over time series.
- [CIRCA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.05871) builds a causal Bayesian network from knowledge of the system architecture and looks for metrics whose distribution changed given their parents in that graph, which is a precise statement of what the frontier rule approximates. On a real-world dataset it improved top-1 recall by 25 percent over the best baseline.
- [RCAEval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.17015) collects 735 failure cases and fifteen reproducible baselines, which is the honest way to find out how far any of this generalizes.

Google's monitoring chapter takes the conservative side on purpose: they avoid systems that try to learn thresholds or detect causality automatically, and keep the path from page to human simple and comprehensible.

blocks.question: Pricing is anomalous and so is catalog, which pricing calls. A junior engineer proposes rolling back pricing, since pricing is where the user-visible errors are counted. What does the frontier rule say?
options: Roll back pricing: it is the service returning errors, so it owns the symptom
Roll back both at once to save time
Pricing's anomaly is already explained by its anomalous dependency, so it is not a candidate until catalog is ruled out
Neither is a candidate, because both are anomalous
blocks.explain: The frontier keeps only anomalous nodes whose dependencies are healthy. Pricing's slowness is fully accounted for by waiting on catalog, and rolling back pricing changes nothing about the catalog queue while adding a second change to reason about. Rolling back both at once also destroys your ability to attribute the recovery to either one.

blocks.question: Your service map has no edge between cart and catalog, yet during an incident both are anomalous and both are on the frontier. What is the most likely explanation worth checking first?
options: A hidden shared dependency (same hosts, same cache, same config push) that is not drawn in the map
Two independent faults at the same moment
The frontier rule does not apply to services with multiple callers
Granger causality between the two metric streams
blocks.explain: Two simultaneous frontier nodes usually mean one missing edge, not two faults. Shared infrastructure is the common culprit, and checking it is cheap: look for a resource, host set, or recent change the two have in common. Two genuinely independent faults do happen, but they are the less likely hypothesis, and the troubleshooting chapter's advice applies: when you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras.

lessons.title: What touched it last: change correlation and bisection

blocks.md:
The SRE troubleshooting chapter puts it as a law of inertia: a working system tends to stay working until an external force acts on it, such as a configuration change or a shift in load. So recent changes are a productive place to start, which is why mature systems log every deploy, config push and package change, and annotate dashboards with deploy start and end times.

In our incident two changes landed in the window. A cart deploy at 20:09, and a catalog config push at 20:14 that rendered the connection pool as 4 instead of 64.

scenes.caption: The change log for the window. Two candidates, five minutes apart. Both teams are now in the incident channel saying it was not them.
Overlay the anomalies. All four lanes break at the same instant and recover together, which tells you they are one event, not four.

Align the edges. The first deviation is 12 seconds after the catalog push (the time for the queue to fill to the timeout) and 5 minutes 12 seconds after the cart deploy. Nothing happened in those five minutes.

The revert at 20:27 is the second half of the proof: the pool returns to 64, the queue drains and all four lanes clear within two minutes. A change that both starts and stops the symptom is hard to argue with.

blocks.md:
Time alignment is strong evidence because changes are rare compared to the resolution of your clock. Cloudflare's write-up gives a usable rate: 476 change requests to WAF managed rules in 60 days, about one every three hours. At that rate the expected number of unrelated changes landing in any given minute is 0.0055, so a change in the same minute as a step change in a metric is not a coincidence you should shrug at.

This is why the change log is the first thing to open, and why change events belong on the same graph as the signals rather than in a separate tool.

A change correlating in time is still only a correlation. Cloudflare's team initially suspected an attack of a kind they had never seen, and only ruled it out at 14:00 by pulling live CPU data from a machine, confirming with strace, and reading error logs. They then ran what they call negative tests, asking whether it really was that particular change, before trusting the conclusion. Confirm with a mechanism, not just a timestamp.

When the window holds many changes instead of two, stop guessing and bisect. Bisection is the same divide-and-conquer the troubleshooting chapter recommends for layered systems, applied to a sequence of changes: test the middle one, learn which half contains the first bad change, repeat.

Identifying one bad change out of $N$ candidates takes about $\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ tests. Git prints exactly this when you bisect: "Bisecting: 337 revisions left to test after this (roughly 9 steps)", and $\lceil \log_2 337 \rceil = 9$.

blocks.caption: Linear search over a day of changes is 128 tests in the worst case; bisection is 7. The cost is that each test must be run, so the win is real only when a single test is cheap and decisive.

blocks.title: Bisecting 16 config renders on one canary pod
blocks.code:
# 16 rendered catalog configs between the last known good one and now.
# A test applies one render to a single canary pod and reads its p99.
lo, hi = 1, 16          # r1 is known good, r16 is known bad
tests = 0
while hi - lo > 1:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    apply_render(mid, pod="catalog-canary")
    bad = p99_ms("catalog-canary") > 200
    tests += 1
    if bad:
        hi = mid           # first bad change is at or before mid
    else:
        lo = mid           # everything up to mid is good
print("first bad render:", hi, "in", tests, "tests")

scenes.caption: Start with an interval you know brackets the answer: r1 was serving fine, r16 is serving the fault. Everything in between is a candidate.
First test: render r8 on one canary pod. p99 is 13 ms, so r8 is good and the first bad render is above it.
lo moves to 8. Eight candidates left, and one test has removed half the search space.
Second test: r12 gives p99 1000 ms on the canary. Bad, so hi moves to 12 and the answer is in (8, 12].
Third test: r10 is good, lo moves to 10. Fourth test: r11 is bad, hi moves to 11, the interval is one wide and the loop exits.
Four tests for sixteen candidates, matching the ceiling of log2(16). r11 is the render that changed the pool from 64 to 4.

blocks.md:
Bisection has preconditions, and every one of them fails somewhere in production:

- **Monotonicity.** The property must be good before the change and bad after, every time. A flaky or load-dependent symptom makes a test lie, and one lie sends the search into the wrong half. Git exposes `git bisect skip` for untestable points and `git bisect run` for scripted tests precisely because tests are imperfect.
- **A decisive test.** Here one canary pod reproduces the fault, because the pool is per pod. A fault that only appears at full production load has no cheap test, and bisection costs a real outage per step.
- **A sequence.** Deploys are ordered; config pushes from three systems and a feature flag flipped by a dashboard are not. If you cannot order your changes, you cannot bisect them, which is an argument for putting all of them through one log.
- **No interacting changes.** If two changes are jointly required to break the system, bisection finds the second one and calls it the cause.

blocks.prompt: Your symptom only appears above 300 rps, and your canary pod receives 1 percent of traffic. What happens if you bisect using the canary test anyway?
blocks.reveal: Every test comes back good, including the render that is actually bad, so the search converges on r16 and blames the most recent change. A test that cannot reproduce the fault does not return "unknown", it returns "good", and bisection trusts it. Fix the test first: reproduce the fault at canary scale (here, scale the pool down in proportion so utilization matches), or bisect by traffic percentage with a feature flag instead of by change.

blocks.question: You can bisect 128 deploys in 7 tests, each costing one minute of degraded traffic on 1 percent of users. Your incident is a full outage. What is the right order of operations?
options: Bisect immediately: finding the cause is the fastest route to recovery
Bisect, but skip the tests that would affect users
Roll back all 128 deploys at once, then bisect to find the cause at leisure if the rollback worked
Mitigate first (roll back to the last known good state or shed the broken path), then bisect afterwards with no user impact
blocks.explain: During a full outage, 7 minutes spent bisecting is 7 minutes of outage, and the troubleshooting chapter is explicit that stopping the bleeding comes first. Rolling everything back is a legitimate mitigation, but on its own it omits the ordering that matters: mitigate, then investigate on a canary while users are served.

blocks.question: Changes are rare (about one per three hours in the relevant subsystem) and your metric broke 12 seconds after a config push. Which statement is accurate?
options: The near-coincidence is unlikely by chance, so the push is now the leading hypothesis and should be tested by reverting it or reproducing its effect
The 12 second gap proves causation, since the expected number of unrelated changes per minute is 0.0055
The gap is too short: a real config change takes minutes to propagate, so this must be something else
The push can be dismissed, because the first alert did not fire until two minutes later
blocks.explain: Rarity makes the coincidence informative, not conclusive: it promotes the push to the leading hypothesis, which you then test by mechanism (does a pool of 4 saturate at 360 rps?) and by reverting. Rarity bounds coincidence; it does not establish a mechanism, so the option claiming proof overclaims. The 12 second gap is what the model predicts for the queue to fill, and alert delay is a property of your alerting window.

blocks.md:
Time to resolution is not one number, it is four intervals, and they have different fixes.

- **Detect**: fault starts until a human knows. Fixed by alerting on symptoms your users feel, not causes.
- **Triage**: knowing until you know enough to act. This is where the techniques in lessons 1 to 4 live.
- **Mitigate**: acting until users stop feeling it. Fixed by having a rollback, a kill switch, a drain or a fallback that you have used before.
- **Resolve**: users are fine until the system is actually correct again, which may be days later.

Only the first three are in the outage. Resolve is in the postmortem.

blocks.caption: Our incident: push 20:14, page 20:16, candidate found 20:22, revert 20:27 and errors stop, all signals clear 20:29.

blocks.title: Where the minutes go, in two incidents

scenes.caption: Our incident. Two minutes to detect, six to triage, seven to mitigate: 15 minutes, of which 13 were user-visible errors.
Cloudflare, 2 July 2019: deploy 13:42, first page 13:45, WAF identified as the component at 14:00, global kill executed 14:07, traffic normal 14:09. A 27 minute outage.
In both incidents triage dominates, and in both the mitigation started before anyone understood the mechanism. The regular expression that backtracked was analysed long after traffic was restored.

Resolve runs off the right edge. Cloudflare re-enabled the WAF at 14:52, 70 minutes after the push, after running negative and positive tests in one city on non-paying traffic. Our pool fix shipped the next day.

blocks.md: Mitigation comes before understanding. The troubleshooting chapter says your first instinct in a major outage is to hunt the root cause, and to ignore that instinct: make the system work as well as it can under the circumstances, because you are not helping users if the system dies while you are root-causing. The incident management chapter states the priority order directly: stop the bleeding, restore service, preserve the evidence.

The cost of a slow triage is countable. At 2000 rps with 1.33 percent of edge requests failing for 13 minutes, this incident lost about 20,800 requests. Every minute shaved off triage is worth about 1600 of them.

That arithmetic is also why mitigations are prepared in advance. Cloudflare had a built-in global terminate for a single component; our team had a config revert. Neither required knowing why. The slow part of Cloudflare's mitigation was not the decision, taken at 14:02, but reaching the internal control panel: their own Access service was down, some engineers' credentials had been disabled for disuse, and they had to fall back to a rarely used bypass. A mitigation you have never exercised is a hypothesis, not a plan.

Mitigating destroys evidence. Reverting the config drains the queue, restarts pods and rotates the logs that held the smoking gun. Before you revert, spend the 30 seconds: snapshot the pool metrics, grab one stack dump, copy the rendered config, note the exact timestamps. The chapter's phrase is that rapid triage does not preclude preserving evidence of what is going wrong.

Two structural notes on the human side, from the incident management chapter. Separate the roles: an incident commander who holds the state and does not touch the system, an operations lead who is the only one changing it, and a communications role. And declare early. Their rule of thumb is that an event is an incident if a second team is needed, if it is customer visible, or if an hour of concentrated analysis has not solved it.

blocks.question: A team reduced detection from 8 minutes to 1 by alerting on every service's CPU, queue depth and pool wait. Their mean time to resolution got worse. What most likely happened?
options: Detection and triage are independent, so this cannot happen
More alerts means more deduplication work in Alertmanager, which delays notification
Cause-based alerts detect faster but page more often and from more places, so the alert storm grew and triage took longer than the detection saved
Alerting on saturation is always wrong
blocks.explain: Cause-based alerting trades triage time for detection time, and the trade is often bad: every service that is merely a victim now pages too. The SLO-based pattern is to page on the symptom your users feel and keep the cause-level signals as unpaged context, which is exactly what lesson 1 did with 9 groups and 1 page. Saturation signals are valuable; paging a human on each of them is the problem.

blocks.question: At 20:22 you are 90 percent sure catalog's pool config is the cause but you do not know how the value 4 got rendered. What do you do?
options: Keep digging until you understand the rendering, so the revert cannot make things worse
Revert the config now, confirm the symptom clears, and work out how the value got rendered afterwards
Raise the pool to 128 to add margin, since you are unsure of the right value
Wait for the config owner to wake up, since they can explain the render
blocks.explain: Reverting to a state the system ran in minutes ago is the lowest-risk action available, and the recovery is itself evidence for your hypothesis. Understanding the template can happen with users served. Raising the pool to 128 sounds prudent but changes to an untested value, and waiting for the config owner extends a user-visible outage for a conversation.

lessons.title: Trigger, proximate cause, contributing factors, action items

blocks.md:
The incident is over at 20:29. Now the words matter, because the words decide which fixes get funded.

- **Trigger**: the event that started this instance. Here, the catalog config push at 20:14. Google's postmortem template carries a Trigger field separately for this reason; their worked example reads "Latent bug triggered by sudden increase in traffic".
- **Proximate cause**: the mechanism that turned the trigger into user harm. Here, a connection pool of 4 gives catalog a capacity of 333 requests per second against an offered 360, so the queue grows until requests are shed at the 1000 ms timeout.
- **Contributing factors**: the conditions that let the trigger exist, let the harm propagate, or made the response slow. None of them caused the outage alone, and removing any one of them would have changed it.

Our contributing factors, each one a real sentence about the system:

1. The rendered config was applied without validation, so a pool of 4 was deployable at all.
2. Catalog's latency was never split into pool wait and query time, so the one decisive measurement had to be found by hand during triage.
3. Pricing had no fallback for a failed catalog call; a stale cached price would have made this a latency event instead of an availability event.
4. Checkout fails the whole order when pricing fails, so a 7.41 percent dependency error became a 2.96 percent order failure rate.
5. A cart deploy landed five minutes earlier, and cart had a latency alert tight enough to fire, which cost about six minutes of triage.
6. Per-pod alert rules turned one fault into 397 alerts.

scenes.caption: The spine of the story: a trigger, a mechanism, a symptom. This is the part a single-cause writeup would stop at.
Conditions that made the failure possible at all. Neither is a cause on its own; both are necessary for this incident to look like this.
Conditions that made it last longer. These do not appear anywhere in a causal chain of the fault, yet they own most of the 15 minutes.
Now attach one action item to each condition. Each badge is a change that removes a named condition, which is why they are testable and reviewable.
Compare with a single-cause writeup: one action item, aimed at the person who pushed. The same incident with a different vocabulary produces a different fix list.

blocks.md: "The root cause" is usually a decision about where to stop asking, not a fact. The SRE book is careful here: systems are complex, and it is likely that multiple factors, each individually not the cause, are jointly causes. Its template says Root Causes, plural. Note that a cause chain pointing at a person is a sign you stopped one question early.

This is the heart of [John Allspaw's critique of the Five Whys](https://www.kitchensoap.com/2014/11/14/the-infinite-hows/): asking "why" repeatedly tends to terminate at a person's attributes, because each answer is judged with hindsight and each step allows only one question. Their suggested replacement is to ask *how*: how did the people involved go about the change, how did they gain confidence it was safe, what trade-offs did they manage, what time pressure were they under. Those questions produce a narrative with operational detail in it, which is what you can act on.

The related distinction, from human factors research, is between first and second stories. A first story treats human error as the cause of failure and ends with what someone should have done. A second story treats it as the effect of deeper systemic vulnerabilities. Here the first story is "an engineer pushed a bad pool value". The second is "a template rendered a value no one read, a system accepted it without validation, and nothing measured the resource it governed".

Blamelessness is a practical requirement, not a courtesy. A blamelessly written postmortem assumes everyone involved had good intentions and did the right thing with the information they had, and identifies contributing causes without indicting anyone; where blame and shaming prevail, people stop bringing problems to light at all. Etsy's [Debriefing Facilitation Guide](https://extfiles.etsy.com/DebriefingFacilitationGuide.pdf) by John Allspaw, Morgan Evans and Daniel Schauenberg is built around this: it has sections on talking to the people who would usually be blamed, on looking for descriptions rather than explanations, and on the goal being to learn rather than to produce remediation items.

Then write action items that actually reduce recurrence. Google's example postmortem gives each one a type (prevent, mitigate or process), an owner, and a tracking bug, and the review asks whether the causes were understood deeply enough and whether the action plan is prioritized appropriately. Three tests before you accept an item:

- Does it name a condition from your list, or is it an attitude ("be more careful", "add more alerts")?
- Does it remove a class of failure or just this instance? Validating the rendered pool size against a minimum removes every future bad render, not one.
- Is it the kind of thing someone will do? An owner, a bug and a priority, or it is a wish. An unowned item is how incidents recur ad infinitum.

The one thing to keep: triage narrows, mitigation buys time, and the postmortem is where the next incident gets cheaper. Each of the three uses a different artifact: the dependency graph and the distributions for narrowing, a rehearsed rollback or kill switch for mitigating, and a list of named conditions with owners for not doing it again.

blocks.question: Which of these action items from our incident is most likely to prevent a recurrence of the same class of failure?
options: Add a dashboard panel for catalog pool wait time
Require a second reviewer on catalog config changes
Add an alert on catalog p99 latency above 200 ms
Validate the rendered config against a schema that rejects a pool below the measured requirement, and fail the push
blocks.explain: The schema check removes the class: no rendered config below the needed pool size can ever be applied, by any person, at any hour. The dashboard and the p99 alert shorten detection and triage, which is valuable but reactive. A second reviewer adds a human check to a value that was machine-generated and was not read by the first human either, which is exactly the kind of item that feels responsible and changes nothing.

blocks.question: A reviewer rejects the postmortem because the Root Cause field says three things. Based on how the SRE book and Allspaw's writing treat causes, what is the better response?
options: Keep all three: complex systems fail from several conditions that are individually insufficient and jointly sufficient, which is why the field is plural and each condition gets an action item
Pick the earliest event in the timeline, since it caused the others
Pick the one with the most direct mechanism and list the others as background
Rewrite it as a chain of five whys so the single deepest cause becomes clear
blocks.explain: The troubleshooting chapter notes that multiple factors may each be insufficient yet jointly causal, Google's template says Root Causes, and Allspaw's objection to the Five Whys is precisely that a linear chain forces a single terminal cause, usually a person. Picking the earliest event or the most vivid mechanism discards the conditions whose removal would have changed the outcome.

blocks.question: Your organisation writes excellent postmortems and the same class of incident keeps recurring. Which measurement would tell you where the process is leaking?
options: Mean time to resolution for the recurring class
Number of postmortems written per quarter
The fraction of action items with an owner, a bug and a priority that were completed, broken down by type
Number of alerts fired per incident
blocks.explain: Writing the document is not the mechanism that reduces recurrence; completing the typed, owned, tracked items is. Counting postmortems measures effort, and MTTR measures response rather than prevention. If completion is low, the leak is in prioritisation; if completion is high and recurrence continues, the items are not naming the right conditions.
